title: A NATURE IN THE SPACE DESIGN GUIDE FOR STRESS RELIEF THROUGH BIOPHILIC DESIGN
central_proposition: Biophilic design, specifically focusing on the 'nature in the space' category, can be translated into a practical design guide for architects to create stress-relieving environments by integrating specific design patterns and parameters that engage multiple senses and natural processes.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia
concept_definitions.definition: our innate attraction to the patterns and processes of nature

concept_definitions.name: Biophilic design
concept_definitions.definition: draws on our biologically ingrained tendency to interact with and experience nature

concept_definitions.name: Nature in the space
concept_definitions.definition: involves the direct presence of nature in a space, including plant life, water, and animals, as well as natural elements like breezes, sounds, and scents

concept_definitions.name: Stress relief
concept_definitions.definition: direct relief of physical and psychological stress and indirect relief of physical and psychological stress symptoms

concept_definitions.name: In-between place
concept_definitions.definition: an abstract space in architecture with an intermediate relationship between solid... contains the transition of functions

argument_structure: The paper establishes the problem of human disconnection from nature leading to stress, then introduces biophilia and biophilic design as a solution. It focuses on the 'nature in the space' category, identifying six specific design patterns. For each pattern, it outlines its influence on stress relief, general experience, induced symptoms, and design goals. This information is synthesized into a 'toolbox' with main design criteria and parameters, and its application is demonstrated through a prototype case study.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is that humans possess an innate biological connection to nature (biophilia). When this connection is fostered through biophilic design, particularly by directly integrating natural elements and processes ('nature in the space') into built environments, it triggers physiological and psychological restorative responses. These responses lead to reduced stress, improved cognitive function, and enhanced mood. Specific mechanisms are pattern-dependent, such as visual connections reducing eye strain, multisensory engagement providing holistic restoration, and dynamic light regulating circadian rhythms. The overall logic is that re-establishing beneficial human-nature interaction counteracts the negative effects of modern urban disconnection.

findings.antecedent: Disconnection from nature (urban environment)
findings.mechanism: Modern urban environments separate humans from their innate connection to nature, leading to negative physiological and psychological outcomes.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: People are becoming disconnected from nature, mainly due to the urban environment, resulting in high stress levels in modern society.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (using biophilia)
findings.mechanism: Biophilia, as an innate attraction to nature, when integrated into design, leverages this natural tendency to promote restorative effects.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Biophilia, our innate attraction to the patterns and processes of nature, is used by biophilic designs to reduce stress.

findings.antecedent: Nature in the space (direct presence of plant life, water, animals, breezes, sounds, scents)
findings.mechanism: Direct sensory engagement with natural elements and processes in a space triggers restorative physiological and psychological responses.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Nature in the space involves the direct presence of nature in a space, including plant life, water, and animals, as well as natural elements like breezes, sounds, and scents.

findings.antecedent: Designing for multiple sensory experiences (through natural and living processes)
findings.consequent: Effective integration of nature into built environment / Stress relief
findings.mechanism: Engaging multiple senses (visual, auditory, olfactory, haptic, gustatory) creates a more immersive and holistic connection with nature, enhancing restorative outcomes.
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Designing for multiple sensory experiences through natural and living processes is crucial.

findings.antecedent: Disconnection from nature (urban environments, prioritizing technology/indoor activities)
findings.consequent: Compromised attention and self-control, stressful and busy life
findings.mechanism: Lack of natural stimuli leads to a 'stimulus-seeking strategy' that depletes cognitive resources needed for attention and self-control.
findings.source: Section 1. Introduction
findings.quote: This leads to a stimulus-seeking strategy that compromises attention and self-control, resulting in a stressful and busy life (Joye et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Neglecting innate connection to the natural world
findings.consequent: Harm to body, mind, and spirit (human stress levels)
findings.mechanism: Humans have a fundamental biological need for nature; its absence leads to allostatic load and negative health outcomes across multiple domains.
findings.source: Section 1. Introduction
findings.quote: growing evidence shows that our innate connection to the natural world is crucial for human stress levels. Neglecting this need will harm our body, mind, and spirit.

findings.antecedent: Biophilia (innate attraction to nature's patterns and processes)
findings.consequent: Captivation by natural sounds (crackling fires, crashing waves)
findings.mechanism: Biologically ingrained tendencies lead to automatic attention and engagement with specific natural stimuli that were historically relevant for survival or well-being.
findings.source: Section 2.1 Biophilia
findings.quote: Biophilia explains why the sound of crackling fires and crashing waves captivate us...

findings.antecedent: Garden view
findings.mechanism: Exposure to nature, even through a view, provides mental restoration and soft fascination, freeing up cognitive resources for creative thought.
findings.source: Section 2.1 Biophilia
findings.quote: ...how a garden view enhances our creativity...

findings.antecedent: Interactions with animals and walks in parks
findings.mechanism: Direct engagement with living systems and physical activity in natural settings promotes physiological and psychological recovery from stress and fatigue.
findings.source: Section 2.1 Biophilia
findings.quote: ...why interactions with animals and walks in parks have restorative effects.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: By integrating nature into the built environment, biophilic design aligns with human biological tendencies, promoting physiological and psychological relaxation.
findings.source: Section 2.2 Biophilic design
findings.quote: Biophilic design has been shown to reduce stress...

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Nature exposure through biophilic design reduces mental fatigue and provides opportunities for soft fascination, thereby restoring directed attention and improving cognitive performance.
findings.source: Section 2.2 Biophilic design
findings.quote: ...enhance cognitive functions...

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Similar to cognitive function enhancement, biophilic design fosters a mentally restorative state conducive to creative ideation.
findings.source: Section 2.2 Biophilic design
findings.quote: ...promote creativity...

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Holistic integration of nature supports overall physical and mental health, leading to a greater sense of well-being.
findings.source: Section 2.2 Biophilic design
findings.quote: ...improve well-being...

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Exposure to nature in healing environments reduces stress, pain perception, and improves recovery rates, likely through physiological and psychological restoration.
findings.source: Section 2.2 Biophilic design
findings.quote: ...aid healing.

findings.antecedent: Stress
findings.consequent: Inhibition of crucial hormones (that combat heart diseases, depression, anxiety)
findings.mechanism: Chronic stress activates the HPA axis, leading to sustained high cortisol levels which can suppress beneficial hormones and contribute to various health issues.
findings.source: Section 2.3 Stress relief
findings.quote: the primary detrimental effect of stress is its inhibition of crucial hormones that combat heart diseases, depression, and anxiety.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Exposure to nature through biophilic design promotes a sense of safety and calm, reducing threat responses and negative emotional states.
findings.source: Section 2.3 Stress relief
findings.quote: Biophilic design has a lot of stress-reducing effects, leading to positive changes in reduced levels of negatively toned emotions (fear, anger)...

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.mechanism: Nature exposure triggers reward pathways and aesthetic appreciation, leading to increased feelings of pleasantness and positive affect.
findings.source: Section 2.3 Stress relief
findings.quote: ...elevated positive emotions (pleasantness)...

findings.antecedent: Viewing nature (in natural environments and laboratories)
findings.consequent: Physiological indicators (blood pressure, heart activity, muscle tension)
findings.mechanism: Nature scenes activate the parasympathetic nervous system, promoting relaxation and physiological recovery from stress.
findings.source: Section 2.3 Stress relief
findings.quote: ...viewing nature can quickly restore physiological indicators like blood pressure, heart activity, and muscle tension within three to five minutes (Kellert et al., 2011).

findings.antecedent: Initially stressed individuals (viewing nature)
findings.consequent: Therapeutic effects (positive physiological and emotional changes)
findings.mechanism: Individuals with higher baseline stress levels have a greater capacity for physiological and psychological restoration when exposed to nature, demonstrating a stronger therapeutic effect.
findings.source: Section 2.3 Stress relief
findings.quote: Notably, initially stressed individuals experience the most significant therapeutic effects regarding positive physiological and emotional changes (Ulrich, 1999).

findings.antecedent: Integrating nature into the in-between place (transition zones in buildings)
findings.mechanism: Transition spaces, often associated with cognitive load, become restorative when infused with nature, offering a mental break and reducing stress during functional shifts.
findings.source: Section 3. Nature in the Space
findings.quote: This makes it a perfect place to distract the mind by integrating nature into the space, thus providing stress relief.

findings.antecedent: Complexity and order pattern (natural analogues category)
findings.mechanism: Visual environments with symmetries, fractal geometries, and coherent spatial hierarchy, similar to nature, provide processing fluency and reduce cognitive load, leading to positive stress responses.
findings.source: Section 3. Nature in the Space
findings.quote: The natural analogues category's complexity and order pattern positively impacts perceptual and physiological stress responses, as shown in Appendix 1.

findings.antecedent: Excessive or prolonged exposure to high-fractal dimensions
findings.mechanism: While moderate fractal patterns are restorative, overly complex or unpredictable visual information can overwhelm cognitive processing, leading to negative affective states.
findings.source: Section 3. Nature in the Space
findings.quote: Striking a balance is crucial, as excessive or prolonged exposure to high-fractal dimensions can cause discomfort or fear...

findings.antecedent: Avoiding or underutilising fractals
findings.mechanism: Environments lacking natural complexity or variability become monotonous, failing to engage attention and leading to boredom and disinterest.
findings.source: Section 3. Nature in the Space
findings.quote: ...while avoiding or underutilising fractals may result in predictability and disinterest (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Prospect pattern (nature of the space category)
findings.mechanism: Unobstructed views over a distance allow for surveillance and planning, providing a sense of safety and control, which reduces stress.
findings.source: Section 3. Nature in the Space
findings.quote: The prospect pattern of the nature of the space category can relieve stress, as shown in Appendix 1.

findings.antecedent: Visual connection with nature (views of natural elements, living systems, processes)
findings.consequent: Attention, stimulation, calmness, sense of time/weather/living entities
findings.mechanism: Visual access to nature provides rich, dynamic, yet non-threatening stimuli that engage attention, offer mental restoration, and connect individuals to natural cycles.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: A space with a strong visual connection with nature captures attention, evokes stimulation or calmness, and conveys a sense of time, weather, and other living entities (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Visual connection with nature pattern
findings.mechanism: Exposure to nature views triggers physiological and psychological relaxation responses, leading to a reduction in perceived stress.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: The visual connection with nature pattern is based on research showing reduced stress...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kellert et al., 2011; Terrapin Bright Green, 2014

findings.antecedent: Visual connection with nature pattern
findings.mechanism: Nature views promote positive affect and reduce negative emotions, contributing to better emotional regulation.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: ...improved emotional functioning...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kellert et al., 2011; Terrapin Bright Green, 2014

findings.antecedent: Visual connection with nature pattern
findings.mechanism: Nature views provide opportunities for soft fascination and mental restoration, reducing directed attention fatigue and improving the ability to concentrate and recover from cognitive demands.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: ...enhanced concentration and recovery rates when exposed to nature views...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kellert et al., 2011; Terrapin Bright Green, 2014

findings.antecedent: Office workers with a window view of nature
findings.mechanism: Regular exposure to nature views provides micro-restorative breaks, reducing cumulative stress and its physical manifestations.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Office workers with a window view of nature reported significantly fewer physical complaints, as shown in Figure 5, and lower frustration, higher life satisfaction, and better overall health (Kellert et al., 2011).

findings.antecedent: Lack of access to nature
findings.mechanism: Disconnection from nature deprives individuals of restorative stimuli, contributing to cognitive and emotional distress.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Lack of access to nature can lead to confusion and anxiety (Kellert, 2018).

findings.antecedent: Visual connections with nature
findings.consequent: Mood, self-esteem, blood pressure, heart rate, attention, happiness
findings.mechanism: Nature views trigger a cascade of positive physiological and psychological responses, including parasympathetic activation and positive emotional shifts.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Visual connections with nature positively affect mood, self-esteem, blood pressure, heart rate, attention, and happiness.

findings.antecedent: Experiencing nature (e.g., exercise in green space) for first five minutes
findings.mechanism: Even brief exposure to nature can rapidly induce positive affective states and improve self-perception.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Experiencing nature, such as through exercise in a green space, positively impacts mood and self-esteem within the first five minutes (Ulrich, 1999; Barton & Pretty, 2010).

findings.antecedent: Viewing nature for ten minutes (before a mental stressor)
findings.consequent: Heart rate variability and parasympathetic activity
findings.mechanism: Pre-exposure to nature primes the body's parasympathetic system, enhancing its ability to cope with subsequent stressors.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Viewing nature for ten minutes before a mental stressor stimulates heart rate variability and parasympathetic activity (Brown et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: High heart rate variability
findings.mechanism: High HRV indicates a healthy and flexible autonomic nervous system, reflecting better stress regulation and overall physiological resilience.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: High heart rate variability enables the body to function optimally...

findings.antecedent: Parasympathetic nervous system
findings.mechanism: The parasympathetic system is responsible for 'rest and digest' functions, promoting recovery and energy conservation.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: ...while the parasympathetic nervous system facilitates relaxation and recuperation after physical activity (Brown et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Viewing a forest scene for 20 minutes (after a mental stressor)
findings.mechanism: Nature exposure reduces physiological arousal and shifts brain activity towards a more relaxed state, promoting recovery from stress.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Additionally, viewing a forest scene for 20 minutes after a mental stressor relaxes blood flow and brain activity (Tsunetsugu & Miyazaki, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Nature scenes
findings.mechanism: Nature's aesthetic qualities and inherent reward value activate brain regions associated with pleasure, leading to positive emotional experiences.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Nature scenes stimulate more pleasure receptors in the brain, leading to prolonged interest and faster stress recovery (Tsunetsugu & Miyazaki, 2005).

findings.antecedent: High-quality view of natural elements, living systems, and natural processes
findings.mechanism: High-quality nature views allow individuals to shift focus and relax eye muscles, providing mental restoration and reducing cognitive load.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: The design goal for stress relief experience in the natural in-between space is to create an environment that promotes relaxation and reduces cognitive fatigue by allowing individuals to shift their focus and relax their eye muscles (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Increased visibility of biodiversity
findings.consequent: Design goal (stress relief, relaxation, reduced cognitive fatigue)
findings.mechanism: Greater biodiversity provides richer, more engaging, and complex natural stimuli, enhancing the restorative potential of nature views.
findings.source: Section 4.1 Design pattern: Visual connection with nature
findings.quote: In addition, increased visibility of biodiversity is essential.

findings.antecedent: Non-visual connection with nature (sounds, aromas, textures resembling outdoors)
findings.mechanism: Multisensory natural stimuli evoke positive associations and provide a sense of being outdoors, contributing to a feeling of refreshment and harmony.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature
findings.quote: A space with a strong non-visual Connection with nature feels refreshing and harmonious.

findings.antecedent: Experiencing nature through a non-visual connection
findings.consequent: Blood pressure, stress hormones, cognitive performance, mental health
findings.mechanism: Non-visual sensory inputs from nature (auditory, olfactory, haptic) directly influence physiological and neurological systems, promoting relaxation, reducing stress, and enhancing cognitive function.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature
findings.quote: Studies have indicated that experiencing nature through a non-visual connection with nature can positively affect blood pressure, stress hormones, cognitive performance, and mental health (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature sounds
findings.mechanism: Nature sounds provide a low-demand, soft fascination stimulus that allows the brain to recover from directed attention fatigue and stress.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Auditory)
findings.quote: Auditory: Exposure to nature sounds accelerates restoration after a psychological stressor (Alvarsson et al., 2011) and reduces cognitive fatigue (Jahncke et al., 2011).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Alvarsson et al., 2011; Jahncke et al., 2011

findings.antecedent: Listening to river sounds or watching nature movie with river sounds (compared to office noise or silence)
findings.mechanism: Pleasant and engaging natural sounds provide a positive emotional and cognitive boost, counteracting the draining effects of monotonous or stressful auditory environments.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Auditory)
findings.quote: Participants listening to river sounds or watching a nature movie with river sounds reported increased energy and motivation compared to those exposed to office noise or silence (Jahncke et al.,2011).

findings.antecedent: Integrating nature views (with auditory sensory systems)
findings.mechanism: Multisensory congruence between visual and auditory nature stimuli enhances the overall restorative experience and contributes more strongly to well-being.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Auditory)
findings.quote: Also, when integrating nature views, there is a strong connection between our visual and auditory sensory systems and psychological well-being (Hunter et al., 2010).

findings.antecedent: Olfactory exposure to herbs and essential oils from trees
findings.mechanism: Natural scents (phytoncides) have direct physiological effects on the immune system and can trigger limbic responses associated with healing and well-being.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Olfactory)
findings.quote: Olfactory exposure to herbs and essential oils from trees positively affects healing and immune function (Kim et al., 2007; Li et al., 2012).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kim et al., 2007; Li et al., 2012

findings.antecedent: Interactions (pet therapy, gardening, touching real plant life)
findings.mechanism: Haptic engagement with living systems provides tactile sensory input that can be soothing, reduce mental and physical fatigue, and foster a sense of connection and responsibility towards nature.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Haptic)
findings.quote: Haptic: Interactions like pet therapy, gardening, and touching real plant life have calming effects, reduce fatigue, and promote environmental stewardship (Yamane et al., 2004).

findings.antecedent: Touching natural elements (water or raw materials)
findings.mechanism: Haptic interaction with natural, unprocessed materials provides sensory richness and a connection to nature, eliciting similar restorative responses as touching living plants.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature (Haptic)
findings.quote: Likewise, touching natural elements like water or raw materials may have similar health benefits (Koga & Iwasaki, 2013).

findings.antecedent: Non-visual connection with nature (sound, scent, touch, taste)
findings.consequent: Stress, perceived physical and mental health
findings.mechanism: Engaging multiple non-visual senses with nature provides a holistic and immersive experience that directly influences physiological and psychological well-being, reducing stress and promoting health.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature
findings.quote: The design goal for this pattern... is to provide an environment that uses sound, scent, touch and possibly even taste to engage the individual in a manner that helps reduce stress and improve perceived physical and mental health (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Incorporating elements that cohesively engage multiple senses
findings.mechanism: Multisensory congruence and richness amplify the restorative effects of nature, leading to more effective stress reduction and health benefits.
findings.source: Section 4.2 Design pattern: Non-visual connection with nature
findings.quote: To meet the design objective, it is crucial to incorporate elements that cohesively engage multiple senses.

findings.antecedent: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli (unpredictable, fleeting connections with nature)
findings.consequent: Sense of uniqueness, freshness, engagement, stimulation, invigoration, welcomed distraction
findings.mechanism: Brief, unpredictable natural stimuli capture attention without demanding sustained effort, offering micro-restorative breaks and preventing habituation, thereby refreshing the mind.
findings.source: Section 4.3 Design pattern: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli
findings.quote: A space with a strong presence of non-rhythmic sensory stimuli provides a sense of experiencing something unique, fresh, engaging, stimulating, and invigorating. It offers a brief yet welcomed distraction (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Exposure to stochastic movement of objects in nature, natural sounds and scents
findings.mechanism: Unpredictable natural stimuli engage the brain in a way that promotes recovery from mental fatigue and physiological stress, possibly by activating the parasympathetic system.
findings.source: Section 4.3 Design pattern: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli
findings.quote: Studies have shown that exposure to the stochastic movement of objects in nature and natural sounds and scents supports physiological restoration.

findings.antecedent: Prolonged visual focus on a computer screen or task
findings.mechanism: Sustained directed attention on a near-field, static stimulus leads to muscle fatigue in the eyes and cognitive depletion.
findings.source: Section 4.3 Design pattern: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli
findings.quote: For example, prolonged visual focus on a computer screen or a task can cause eye strain and fatigue.

findings.antecedent: Periodic breaks with brief visual or auditory distractions (looking up > 20 seconds, focusing on distant point > 20 feet)
findings.mechanism: Shifting gaze to a distant, non-demanding stimulus allows the ciliary muscles of the eye to relax (accommodative rest), reducing eye strain and promoting visual recovery.
findings.source: Section 4.3 Design pattern: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli
findings.quote: However, taking periodic breaks with brief visual or auditory distractions, where one looks up (for > 20 seconds) and focuses on a distant point (of > 20 feet), allows the muscles to relax and the lenses to flatten (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Natural sensory stimuli (unobtrusively attracting attention)
findings.mechanism: Brief, non-demanding natural stimuli provide micro-restorative breaks that allow for the replenishment of directed attention and reduction of physiological stress.
findings.source: Section 4.3 Design pattern: Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli
findings.quote: The goal for the natural in-between place related to this pattern is to use natural sensory stimuli that unobtrusively attract attention to replenish focus and reduce mental fatigue and physiological stress (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Thermal and airflow variability (subtle changes mimicking natural environments)
findings.mechanism: Dynamic thermal and airflow conditions prevent monotony, engage interoceptive senses, and provide a sense of naturalness, leading to positive affective and physiological states.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: A good thermal and airflow variability creates a refreshing, active, and comfortable space that invigorates.

findings.antecedent: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.consequent: Sense of flexibility and control (over climate)
findings.mechanism: The ability to adjust one's immediate thermal environment enhances perceived control, which is a known stress-reducer and satisfaction-enhancer.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: In addition, it provides a sense of flexibility and control because the user can adjust the climate of a particular place.

findings.antecedent: Moderate sensory variability (light, sound, temperature)
findings.mechanism: Humans are adapted to dynamic natural environments; moderate variability provides optimal stimulation, preventing boredom without causing overload.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: People prefer moderate sensory variability in the environment, including light, sound and temperature variations.

findings.antecedent: Lack of sensory stimulation and variety in the environment
findings.mechanism: Monotonous environments fail to engage the attention system, leading to under-stimulation and negative affective states.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: When there is a lack of sensory stimulation and variety in the environment, it can result in feelings of boredom and passivity. (Heerwagen, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Soft fascination elements (light breezes)
findings.mechanism: Soft fascination provides a low-demand, engaging stimulus that allows directed attention to rest and recover, thereby improving subsequent concentration and performance.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: According to Kaplan's Attention Restoration Theory, soft fascination elements like light breezes improve concentration, and various thermal conditions can enhance concentration and performance (Heerwagen & Gregory, 2008; Kaplan, 1995; Elzeyadi, 2012).

findings.antecedent: Changes in ventilation velocity
findings.mechanism: Dynamic airflow provides sensory variability that enhances thermal comfort and may stimulate cognitive processes, potentially aiding working memory.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: Changes in ventilation velocity positively impact comfort and may improve access to short-term memory (Wigö, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Thermal and airflow variability (with control over thermal conditions)
findings.consequent: Sensory experience of airflow and thermal variability
findings.mechanism: Allowing users to experience and control dynamic thermal conditions aligns with human adaptive comfort and preference for variability, leading to a more engaging and comfortable environment.
findings.source: Section 4.4 Design pattern: Thermal and airflow variability
findings.quote: The objective of the natural in-between place related to this pattern is to provide users with the sensory experience of airflow and thermal variability along with control over thermal conditions (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Presence of water (sight, sound, touch)
findings.mechanism: Water's multisensory attributes provide rich, dynamic, yet often soothing stimuli that engage multiple senses, making an environment more compelling and stimulating.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Water enhances the place experience through sight, sound, and touch (Ulrich, 1993).

findings.antecedent: Presence of water pattern
findings.consequent: Positive emotional responses and reduced stress
findings.mechanism: Water features evoke a sense of calm, provide soft fascination, and can activate parasympathetic responses, leading to positive emotional states and stress reduction.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: The presence of water pattern is based on research showing positive emotional responses and reduced stress in environments with water elements.

findings.antecedent: Water features
findings.consequent: Heart rate and blood pressure, concentration and memory
findings.mechanism: Water's soothing sounds and visual dynamics can reduce physiological arousal and provide a restorative focus, aiding cognitive functions.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Water features can lower heart rate and blood pressure and improve concentration and memory.

findings.antecedent: Multiple senses stimulated by water
findings.mechanism: Multisensory engagement with water creates a richer, more immersive experience, leading to heightened awareness and more robust responses to the environment.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Multiple senses stimulated by water enhance perception and responsiveness.

findings.antecedent: Nature images with water elements
findings.mechanism: Visual representations of water, even without direct sensory engagement, can trigger similar physiological relaxation responses as real water.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Nature images with water elements reduce blood pressure and heart rate (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Water presence in green spaces
findings.mechanism: The combination of water and greenery provides a more potent restorative effect, enhancing positive self-perception and emotional states.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Water presence in green spaces improves self-esteem and mood compared to green environments without water.

findings.antecedent: Auditory and tactile access to water
findings.mechanism: The sounds and physical sensation of water provide soothing, low-demand stimuli that promote relaxation and reduce physiological stress.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Auditory and tactile access to water also reduces stress (Alvarsson et al., 2010; Pheasant et al., 2010).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Alvarsson et al., 2010; Pheasant et al., 2010

findings.antecedent: Water's appearance and mood (based on sunlight, varying hues and reflections)
findings.mechanism: The dynamic interaction of light with water creates visually engaging and stimulating patterns that enhance the aesthetic experience and connection to natural processes.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: Water's appearance and mood change based on sunlight, with varying hues and reflections. In bright sunlight, water becomes animated, reflecting the surrounding environment with sparkling movements. (Kellert et al., 2011)

findings.antecedent: Presence of flora and fauna (with water)
findings.mechanism: The integration of living systems (plants, animals) with water creates a more complete and ecologically rich natural experience, amplifying the biophilic response.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: The presence of flora and fauna enhances water's significance... In the built environment, adding fish mainly enhances water's biophilic attraction.(Kellert et al., 2011)

findings.antecedent: Presence of water (multisensory attributes)
findings.mechanism: Water's ability to engage multiple senses provides a rich, restorative stimulus that soothes, encourages contemplation, and reduces mental exhaustion.
findings.source: Section 4.5 Design pattern: Presence of water
findings.quote: The Presence of Water pattern aims to enhance the place experience by utilising water's multisensory attributes. It aims to soothe, encourage contemplation, improve mood, and provide restoration from cognitive fatigue (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Dynamic and diffuse light (changing intensities of light and shadow)
findings.mechanism: Natural light variability mimics outdoor conditions, providing visual interest (drama, intrigue) while also promoting a sense of calm through its natural rhythm and soft transitions.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Dynamic and diffuse light creates changing intensities of light and shadow over time, evoking drama, intrigue, and a sense of calm in a space (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Quality daylighting
findings.mechanism: Exposure to natural daylight, especially with appropriate intensity and spectral composition, supports circadian rhythm and neurotransmitter balance, positively influencing mood.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Quality daylighting has been linked to positive moods.

findings.antecedent: Natural light
findings.consequent: Spatial and temporal responses, orientation to surroundings, daylight patterns, seasonal shifts
findings.mechanism: Natural light provides crucial temporal cues for circadian entrainment and spatial cues for perceiving the environment, connecting individuals to the broader natural world.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Natural light affects spatial and temporal responses, orient itself to its surroundings, and relates to daylight patterns and seasonal shifts. (Kellert, 2018)

findings.antecedent: Sunlight changing color (yellow morning, blue midday, red afternoon/evening)
findings.consequent: Body temperature, heart rate, circadian functioning
findings.mechanism: The spectral changes in natural light throughout the day act as powerful zeitgebers, entraining the body's internal clock and influencing physiological processes.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: The body responds to the colour transition of daylight. The response is apparent in body temperature, heart rate, and circadian functioning.

findings.antecedent: Serotonin and melatonin levels (influenced by light)
findings.mechanism: Light exposure, particularly its timing and intensity, regulates the production of serotonin (mood) and melatonin (sleep), which are critical for overall health.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Serotonin and melatonin levels influenced by light impact sleep, mood, and health conditions(Kandel et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Natural daylight variability
findings.consequent: Patients in recovery and mental health treatment
findings.mechanism: Dynamic natural light provides stimulating yet non-overwhelming input that supports mental restoration and physiological healing in vulnerable populations.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Natural daylight variability benefits patients in recovery and mental health treatment.

findings.antecedent: Bright visible light during the day and darkness at night
findings.mechanism: This light-dark cycle is crucial for proper circadian entrainment, which regulates numerous physiological processes vital for health.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Bright visible light during the day and darkness at night is essential for health.

findings.antecedent: Lack of natural light
findings.mechanism: Insufficient natural light disrupts circadian rhythms, leading to sleep disturbances, mood disorders, and impaired cognitive function.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: Lack of natural light can lead to health, performance, and well-being issues (Kellert, 2018).

findings.antecedent: Stimulating lighting options (promoting positive psychological/physiological responses, supporting circadian system functioning)
findings.mechanism: Dynamic and diffuse light, by mimicking natural light patterns, supports healthy circadian rhythms and provides engaging visual stimuli that promote mental and physiological restoration.
findings.source: Section 4.6 Design pattern: Dynamic and diffuse light
findings.quote: The goal for the natural in-between place related to this pattern is to provide stimulating lighting options that promote positive psychological and physiological responses and support circadian system functioning (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Incorporating nature in the in-between place (building cores, transition zones)
findings.consequent: Stress relief, mental break (before next activity)
findings.mechanism: Infusing nature into high-traffic transition areas provides opportunities for brief mental restoration, allowing users to disengage from previous tasks and prepare for new ones with reduced stress.
findings.source: Section 5.1 Natural in-between place
findings.quote: This makes it a very suitable place to incorporate nature in the space and thus stress relief, as users have mentally had a break when they start the next activity.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architects using the proposed 'nature in the space' design guide will report a more effective and structured approach to integrating biophilic elements for stress relief in their design process compared to those without the guide.
Buildings designed using the proposed 'nature in the space' design guide will demonstrate higher levels of occupant-reported stress relief and well-being compared to control buildings.

The integration of the six biophilic design patterns (visual connection with nature, non-visual connection with nature, non-rhythmic sensory stimuli, thermal & airflow variability, presence of water, dynamic & diffuse light) in architectural projects will lead to measurable reductions in physiological stress markers (e.g., cortisol, heart rate) and improvements in cognitive performance among occupants.

Design parameters identified in the guide (high-quality views of natural elements, diversity of nature, flowing clean water, short versus long exposure, natural light, and shifts throughout the day and season) will correlate with increased stress relief and positive emotional responses in built environments.
bridge_warrants: The design guide translates existing biophilic theories into practical design parameters for architects.
The framework connects biophilic design patterns to stress relief mechanisms, drawing on theories like Attention Restoration Theory and Stress Recovery Theory.
The proposed toolbox integrates design principles with project requirements and vision mapping, bridging theoretical concepts with architectural practice.
model_structure: The paper proposes a hierarchical model for a design guide, structured around a central design criterion: 'Designing high-quality connections with natural processes for multiple senses'. This criterion is supported by six key design parameters: 'High quality view of natural elements', 'Biodiversity', 'Flowing clean water', 'Short exposure vs. long exposure', 'Natural light', and 'Day and seasonal shifts'. These parameters are, in turn, informed by six biophilic design patterns: 'Visual connection with nature', 'Non-visual connection with nature', 'Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli', 'Thermal and airflow variability', 'Presence of water', and 'Dynamic and diffuse light'. This structure forms a 'toolbox' that integrates the design diagram with a plan of requirements and a vision map for project-specific application.
limitations: Architects have not sufficiently tested the use of this design guide to prove that it gives promising results in the design process.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Biophilic design elements facilitate cognitive restoration by providing opportunities for 'soft fascination', thereby reducing mental fatigue and improving directed attention, which contributes to stress relief.

Exposure to natural environments and biophilic elements elicits positive emotional responses and physiological relaxation (e.g., reduced heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol levels), directly contributing to stress reduction.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic design elements in indoor spaces lead to stress relief through perceptual engagement, cognitive restoration, and physiological relaxation.

steps.from_construct: Exposure to biophilic design elements (e.g., natural light, plants, views of nature)
steps.to_construct: Perceptual engagement (e.g., soft fascination, sense of naturalness)
Cognitive restoration (e.g., reduced mental fatigue, improved attention) and/or Physiological relaxation (e.g., reduced sympathetic arousal)
